juli.etymology_derivation: The same Latin month name as English July.

augustus.etymology_derivation: The same Latin month name as English August.

september.etymology_derivation: The same Latin month name as English September.

oktober.etymology_derivation: The same Latin month name as English October.

november.etymology_derivation: The same Latin month name as English November.

december.context_translation: In December it is a celebration.
december.etymology_derivation: The same Latin month name as English December.

honger.etymology_derivation: English hunger and Dutch honger are the same word; Dutch says 'have hunger'.

dorst.etymology_derivation: English thirst and Dutch dorst are the same word; Dutch says 'have thirst'.

liefde.etymology_derivation: English love and Dutch liefde are the same root.

geluk.etymology_derivation: The same root as English luck; Dutch also means happiness.

pijn.etymology_derivation: Latin poena gave English pain and Dutch pijn.

bang.etymology_derivation: The English lookalike bang is unrelated; Dutch bang means afraid.

geld.etymology_derivation: English geld is archaic; Dutch geld is everyday money.

winkel.etymology_derivation: German Winkel means corner; Dutch narrowed it to shop.

werk.etymology_derivation: The same word as English work.

gewicht.etymology_derivation: English weight and Dutch gewicht are the same noun; gh/ch correspondence.

baas.etymology_derivation: English boss is a Dutch loan; the circle came back around.

leraar.etymology_derivation: From leren ('teach'); the -aar ending marks the agent.

arts.etymology_derivation: From Latin ars ('art, skill'); Dutch narrowed it to physician.

bakker.etymology_derivation: English baker and Dutch bakker are the same agent noun.

kantoor.etymology_derivation: French comptoir ('counter') gave English counter and Dutch kantoor.

trein.etymology_derivation: The same French loan as English train.

station.etymology_derivation: The same Latin loan as English station.

ticket.etymology_derivation: A recent English loan, little changed.

fiets.etymology_derivation: A Dutch word of uncertain origin; the everyday bicycle.

auto.etymology_derivation: The same clipping of automobile as English auto.

boot.etymology_derivation: English boat and Dutch boot are the same word.

vliegtuig.etymology_derivation: vliegen ('fly') + tuig ('rig'); German uses the same model.

weg.etymology_derivation: English way and Dutch weg are the same word.

brug.etymology_derivation: English bridge and Dutch brug are the same word; English palatalized the g.

kerk.etymology_derivation: Greek kyriakon gave English church and Dutch kerk.

markt.etymology_derivation: The same Latin loan as English market.

glas.etymology_derivation: English glass and Dutch glas are direct twins.

zin.etymology_derivation: English sense is a Latin loan; Dutch zin is the native word for sense/desire.

trek.etymology_derivation: From trekken ('pull'); appetite is a pull toward food.

rekening.etymology_derivation: English reckoning and Dutch rekening are the same noun; Dutch narrowed it to bill.

kosten.etymology_derivation: English cost and Dutch kosten are the same verb.

shirt.etymology_derivation: A recent English loan; Dutch treats it as het.

broek.etymology_derivation: English breeches and Dutch broek are the same word.

blauw.etymology_derivation: French bleu gave English blue and Dutch blauw.

rood.etymology_derivation: English red and Dutch rood are the same word.

groen.etymology_derivation: English green and Dutch groen are the same word.

geel.etymology_derivation: English yellow and Dutch geel are cognate; English y answers to Dutch g here.

wit.etymology_derivation: English white and Dutch wit are the same word.

zwart.etymology_derivation: English swart is archaic; Dutch zwart is everyday black.

bruin.etymology_derivation: English brown and Dutch bruin are the same word.

vers.etymology_derivation: English fresh and Dutch vers are the same word.

vol.etymology_derivation: English full and Dutch vol are the same word.

open.etymology_derivation: The same adjective as English open.

dicht.etymology_derivation: English tight is the old cousin; Dutch dicht means closed.

leeg.etymology_derivation: A Dutch adjective with no close English twin.

nodig.etymology_derivation: From nood ('need'); English need is the same root.

samen.etymology_derivation: English same and Dutch samen share the root; Dutch means together.

buiten.etymology_derivation: English butan is obsolete; Dutch buiten is everyday outside.

thuis.etymology_derivation: A Dutch place word; huis ('house') is inside it.

links.etymology_derivation: The Dutch direction word; English left is unrelated.

rechts.etymology_derivation: English right and Dutch rechts are the same word.

vraag.etymology_derivation: From vragen ('ask'); English ask is a different root.

verhaal.etymology_derivation: A Dutch noun from verhalen ('tell'); no transparent English twin.

feest.etymology_derivation: Latin festa gave English feast and Dutch feest.

room.etymology_derivation: English room is unrelated; Dutch room is cream.

brief.etymology_derivation: English brief and Dutch brief are the same word; Dutch narrowed it to letter.

kop.etymology_derivation: The English lookalike cop is unrelated; Dutch kop is cup or head.

mes.etymology_derivation: English mattock is a distant cousin; Dutch mes is the everyday knife.

zolder.context_translation: The boxes are in the attic.
zolder.etymology_derivation: English solder is unrelated; Dutch zolder is an attic.

broodje.etymology_derivation: Diminutive of brood; every diminutive is het.

kopje.etymology_derivation: Diminutive of kop; the -je makes it het.

huisje.etymology_derivation: Diminutive of huis; the -je makes it het.

appeltje.etymology_derivation: Diminutive of appel; the -tje makes it het.

tafeltje.etymology_derivation: Diminutive of tafel; the -tje makes it het.

bloemetje.etymology_derivation: Diminutive of bloem; the -etje makes it het.

hondje.etymology_derivation: Diminutive of hond; the -je makes it het.

lief.etymology_derivation: English lief is archaic; Dutch lief is everyday sweet/dear.

rustig.etymology_derivation: From rust ('rest'); English rest is the same root.

sch_sh.name: The SCH Bridge
sch_sh.phonetic_rule: English /ʃ/ (sh) corresponds to Dutch /sx/ (sch): ship → schip, shoe → schoen, sheep → schaap.
sch_sh.historical_linguistics: West Germanic *sk stayed a sk-like cluster in Dutch, spelled sch, while English palatalised it to sh.
sch_sh.philological_note: Dutch sch is not English sh; the ch is a voiceless velar fricative. School is a Latin loan shared by both languages.

th_d.name: The TH → D Bridge
th_d.phonetic_rule: English th corresponds to Dutch d: brother → broeder, three → drie, think → denken, thank → danken.
th_d.historical_linguistics: The Germanic dental fricative hardened to a stop in Dutch and German; English kept the fricative.
th_d.philological_note: Weather/weer is cognate but Dutch lost the d, so it is not a th↔d example. Loans such as theater keep t.

f_v.name: The F → V Bridge
f_v.phonetic_rule: English f often corresponds to Dutch v: father → vader, foot → voet, fish → vis.
f_v.historical_linguistics: Dutch voiced West Germanic f to v in many positions; English kept the voiceless consonant.
f_v.philological_note: Northern Dutch often devoices v to [f], especially in vr-/vl- clusters and word-finally; the spelling keeps the historical v.

s_z.name: The S → Z Bridge
s_z.phonetic_rule: English s often corresponds to Dutch z: sun → zon, sea → zee, salt → zout.
s_z.historical_linguistics: Dutch voiced West Germanic s before vowels; English kept s.
s_z.philological_note: Clusters sn/sm/sl keep s (sneeuw, smal, slapen); loans such as school and straat also keep s.

gh_ch.name: The GH → CH Bridge
gh_ch.phonetic_rule: English gh corresponds to Dutch ch: night → nacht, light → licht, right → recht, eight → acht.
gh_ch.historical_linguistics: English gh and Dutch ch descend from a shared velar fricative; English vocalised or lost it, Dutch kept it.
gh_ch.philological_note: Dutch g is the voiced partner of ch. The two are different sounds, not spelling variants.

vowel_ij.name: The IJ Bridge
vowel_ij.phonetic_rule: Dutch ij is /ɛi/ and often answers to English i/y: ice → ijs, wine → wijn, five → vijf.
vowel_ij.historical_linguistics: The digraph ij spells a Dutch diphthong; English orthography kept a different vowel from the same Germanic stock.
vowel_ij.philological_note: IJ is two letters but one sound. It is not English /aɪ/.

vowel_ui.name: The UI Bridge
vowel_ui.phonetic_rule: Dutch ui is /œy/ and often answers to English ou/ow: house → huis, mouse → muis, out → uit.
vowel_ui.historical_linguistics: Dutch ui spells a front rounded diphthong with no close English equivalent; the English spelling twin is a memory hook.
vowel_ui.philological_note: Do not pronounce ui as two English beats; it is one gliding vowel.

vowel_oe.name: The OE Bridge
vowel_oe.phonetic_rule: Dutch oe is /u/ and often answers to English oo/u in spelling: book → boek, foot → voet, good → goed.
vowel_oe.historical_linguistics: The Dutch digraph oe spells a long /u/; English oo spells several different vowels, so this is a spelling/cognacy bridge.
vowel_oe.philological_note: Dutch oe is /u/, not the /ʊ/ of English book. Read the Dutch spelling and use the Dutch sound.

g_y.name: The G / Y Bridge
g_y.phonetic_rule: English g and some y words correspond to voiced Dutch g: gold → goud, good → goed, yellow → geel.
g_y.historical_linguistics: Dutch kept a velar fricative where English kept a stop or palatalised to y. English year/jaar is y↔j, not y↔g.
g_y.philological_note: Dutch g is a fricative, never the English stop in 'good'.

compounds.lore: kast is a cupboard, not a cast; German uses a book+cupboard compound, but the model is shared.
koel ('cool') is not coal; German uses the same cool+cupboard model.
compounds.example_sentence: De melk ligt in de koelkast.
compounds.example_translation: The milk is in the fridge.

compounds.lore: wonen ('dwell') gives woon-; English wont is the archaic cousin.
compounds.example_sentence: De bank staat in de woonkamer.
compounds.example_translation: The sofa is in the living room.

compounds.lore: The same sick+house model as German Krankenhaus; the head noun huis makes it het.
tuig ('rig, gear') is the second half; German Flugzeug uses the same model.
compounds.example_sentence: Het vliegtuig landt om vijf uur.

compounds.lore: doek is cloth; German Handtuch is the same hand+cloth model.
The diminutive -je makes it het; broodje kaas is a cheese roll.
compounds.example_translation: I am eating a cheese roll.

compounds.lore: schaaf is a plane; a Dutch kitchen staple with a transparent name.
stof ('dust') + zuigen ('suck') + -er; German Staubsauger uses the same model.
was is laundry; wassen is to wash. The compound is transparent.
vaat is dishes; the -wasser agent ending mirrors English -washer.
thee is tea; the pot is the same pot.
tanden is the plural of tand; the head noun borstel makes it de.
zon + -e- + bloem; the same sun+flower image as English.
regen ('rain') + boog ('bow'); the metaphor is shared.
compounds.example_sentence: Na de regen komt een regenboog.
compounds.example_translation: After the rain comes a rainbow.

compounds.lore: vuur ('fire') + toren ('tower'); German Leuchtturm uses light instead of fire.
compounds.example_translation: The lighthouse stands by the sea.

falseFriends.trap_note: A room is kamer; room is cream.
English brood is a nest of young; Dutch brood is bread.
A bell is bel; bellen is to call someone.
A policeman is agent; kop is a cup or a head.
A deer is hert; dier is any animal.
Fleece is vlies or wol; vlees is meat.
The tide is getij; tijd is time.
Solder is soldeer; zolder is an attic.
falseFriends.example_translation: The boxes are in the attic.

falseFriends.trap_note: A stool is kruk; stoel is a chair.
A mess is rommel; mes is a knife.
A ram is ram; raam is a window.
A financial bank is also bank, but in a living room bank is a couch.
falseFriends.example_translation: We are sitting on the couch.

falseFriends.trap_note: An English map is kaart; map is a folder.
falseFriends.example_translation: The folder is on the table.

falseFriends.trap_note: An English brand is merk; brand is a fire.
A bang is knal; bang is afraid.
A gown is japon; gewoon means ordinary or simply.
Sin is zonde; zin is sense or desire, as in zin hebben in.
Luck is geluk; lukken is to succeed or manage.
